# Project Context — IceBot-IOT

---

## Overview

**IceBot-IOT** is a control application for the **Fairino FR5** (6-DOF) robotic arm.

The app accepts a **`.lua` script file** as input and drives the robot to execute the movements defined in that script — joint moves, delays, and other commands supported by the Fairino Controller LUA SDK.

**Sample script**: `workflow/lay_coc.lua` (cup pickup step, generated by FaiRobot Studio).

---

## Terminology

| Term (project) | Meaning |
|----------------|---------|
| **Robot controller** | Edge PC at the store — runs IceBot, `workflow/`, NetBird (cloud→edge ingress) |
| **Fairino arm / control box** | Fairino FR5 controller on LAN @ `192.168.58.2` — executes uploaded Lua, exposes **24V digital outputs (DO)** |
| **Peripheral machine** | Non-arm equipment in the cell (ice cream dispenser, topping feeder, cup dispenser, …) |
| **Custom control board** | Store-built PCB: optocoupler isolation → MCU → stepper driver → stepper motor |
| **Cloud server** | Order & payment API on VPS/cloud |

## Deployment: Robot controller (máy biên)

**Lua scripts and IceBot run on the same machine** — the **robot controller** (edge PC) at the store.

| Component | Location |
|-----------|----------|
| IceBot C# app | **Robot controller** (edge PC) |
| `.lua` workflow files (`workflow/`) | **Same machine** (local disk) |
| NetBird client | **Robot controller** (edge PC) |
| Fairino arm control box | LAN @ `192.168.58.2` |
| Order / payment server | Cloud (VPS) |

Lua files are **synced from cloud** during site setup (see **Lua provisioning** below). At runtime, orders use the **local** `workflow/` copy on the robot controller.

```
Robot controller (edge PC — same machine)
├── IceBot.exe
├── workflow/
│   ├── cup_s.lua
│   └── ...
└── NetBird client

        │ LuaUpload (LAN)
        ▼
Fairino arm control box (192.168.58.2)
        │ 24V DO signals (peripheral trigger)
        ▼
Custom control board(s) → stepper drivers → peripheral machines
```

## Peripheral machine control (điều khiển máy trong hệ thống)

Besides arm motion, the cell includes **peripheral machines** (dispensers, feeders, cup dropper, etc.).

> **Business rule (2026-07-31): every peripheral machine triggers over RS485, and only RS485.**
> There used to be a second option (a DO/24V pulse fired from the Fairino control box, driving a
> custom stepper board) — **that option is gone**. Any machine added to the system from now on
> must have its own RS485 head and a host-side driver (`IMachineTrigger`). There is no DO-trigger
> fallback to reach for anymore. A "machine" that is pure arm motion with no separate physical
> hardware to control (e.g. a tray-placement position) is unaffected — it just registers an
> `IMachineModule` with no `IMachineTrigger`, same as before.

**How it works — direct serial link to the PC.**
The machine's mainboard is connected straight to the robot-controller PC over RS485 (COM port, via a USB-RS485 or RS485 transceiver module). IceBot is the **host** and the machine is the **slave**. The peripheral trigger is **not** an alternative to the arm step — it always **follows** it: the step's `.lua` file runs on the Fairino arm first (arm moves into position, top-to-bottom, IceBot does not care about point names inside the file), and only once that finishes does IceBot open the COM port and speak the machine's serial protocol directly (framing, checksum, timeouts/retries).

```
Workflow step (e.g. "cup_s")
        │
        ▼
FairinoLuaExecutor.RunScript(cup_s.lua)   — arm moves into position, runs top-to-bottom
        │  (arm motion finished — it is now physically in place, e.g. under the cup dropper)
        ▼
IceBot.Machines.MachineRegistry  (step name → machine type, if any)
        │
        ▼
IceBot.Machines.<Machine>Client  (opens COM port, sends the machine's own signal over RS485)
        │
        ▼
Peripheral machine mainboard (e.g. cup-dropping machine, RS485 @ 115200)
```

- **Implemented today**: cup-dropping machine (`docs/301 Cup-Dropping Machine Serial Communication Protocol V0.0.3.md`) and the ice cream dispenser (`docs/Ice Cream Machine (Custom STM32 Controller) Serial Communication Protocol V0.1.md`, RS485 via MAX485 to a custom STM32 board) — both under `code/src/IceBot/Machines/`, both reuse `SerialFrameCodec` since the two protocols share the same frame shape.
- COM port per machine type is site-configured (`MachinePorts` in `config/icebot.site.env`, menu 1.2).
- Every workflow step (`.lua` file) belongs to exactly one machine identifier — there is no such thing as a step with no machine. `MachineRegistry.Modules` is the list of every registered machine (`IMachineModule`), including machines that are pure arm motion with no serial connection.
- `IMachineModule` (base, mandatory) carries identity: `MachineType`, `DisplayName`, `StepNames`. There is no ordering/position field — BE sends orders with the run order already decided (see "Order → queue example" below), so IceBot has no need to sort steps itself.
- `IMachineTrigger : IMachineModule` (optional) is implemented only by machines that are also wired to this PC over RS485 and need a signal sent after their step's `.lua` runs. It requires **two** methods: `Trigger(comPort)` (fire the machine's action) and `TestConnection(comPort)` (open the port, do a real query round-trip, throw on failure — no business-specific parsing needed). `WorkflowRunner`, `ConfigSetupWizard` (COM-port prompts), and the console test menus only look at `MachineRegistry.Modules.OfType<IMachineTrigger>()` — a machine that's pure arm motion just implements `IMachineModule` and is left alone by all of them.
- The `.lua` file itself cannot send this signal (Fairino Lua has no raw serial/UART primitive) — the real signal is always sent from IceBot (C#) over RS485 after the file finishes running.
- To add a new machine: create a `Machines/<MachineName>/` folder with a `<MachineName>Client.cs` (raw RS485 protocol — reuse `SerialFrameCodec` if the frame shape matches) and a `<MachineName>Module.cs` implementing `IMachineTrigger` (`Trigger` + `TestConnection`; see `Machines/CupDropping/` or `Machines/IceCream/` for both), then register one instance in `MachineRegistry.Modules`. `TestConnection` is what makes the machine show up automatically in "Test may > 2 Test ket noi may ngoai vi" once its step name is provisioned — no menu code to write per machine.

### Example — ice cream dispenser (máy kem)

A custom **STM32F103C8T6 (Blue Pill)** board talks to the PC over **RS485** (MAX485 transceiver, 115200 baud), running a bidirectional motor (up = dispense, down = cutoff). Protocol: `docs/Ice Cream Machine (Custom STM32 Controller) Serial Communication Protocol V0.1.md` — same frame shape as the cup-dropping protocol, so it reuses `SerialFrameCodec` as-is. Host-side driver: `IceBot.Machines.IceCream.IceCreamMachineClient`; module: `IceCreamMachineModule` (`IMachineTrigger` + `IMachineDiagnostics`).

| Layer | Role |
|-------|------|
| **Lua script** (`ice_chocolate_s.lua`, etc.) | Arm moves to the dispense pose only |
| **IceBot (C#)** | After the step's `.lua` finishes, opens the COM port and sends Motor Run UP (`0x02`) over RS485 |
| **STM32 custom board** | Slave — receives the framed command, drives the stepper (up/down/stop), replies with status (low-stock/out-of-stock/motor-fault/busy) |

### Signal mapping (site-specific)

| Example machine | Step name | Trigger |
|-----------------|-----------|---------|
| Cup dropper (cup-dropping machine) | `cup_s` | Arm runs `cup_s.lua` into position, then IceBot sends serial command (0x04 Dispense Beverage) over RS485, per `MachineRegistry` |
| Ice cream (chocolate S) | `ice_chocolate_s.lua` | Arm runs the dispense pose, then IceBot sends Motor Run UP (0x02) over RS485 to the STM32 board |
| Topping (kẹo cốm) | `topping_keo_com.lua` | ❌ Not yet implemented — must ship with its own RS485 protocol + driver when added |
| Tray delivery | `deliver_tray.lua` | Arm motion only — no separate peripheral machine, no driver needed |

### Software vs hardware boundaries

| Component | Controls arm joints | Controls RS485 peripherals |
|-----------|--------------------|------------------------------|
| IceBot C# | Indirect (upload Lua) | **Yes** — opens COM port, speaks machine protocol directly (`IceBot.Machines`) |
| Fairino Lua on control box | Yes (`MoveJ`, …) | No |
| Custom board firmware | No | N/A (it's the slave being spoken to) |

**Current IceBot status:** ✅ RS485 trigger implemented for the cup-dropping machine (`IceBot.Machines.CupDropping.CupDroppingMachineClient`, 115200 baud, framed protocol with checksum + retry) and the ice cream dispenser (`IceBot.Machines.IceCream.IceCreamMachineClient`, same frame shape) — `WorkflowRunner` always runs the step's `.lua` file on the arm first, then fires the RS485 trigger once the arm has finished.

**Safety / wiring:** 24V DO must match Fairino electrical specs; use optocoupler isolation between controller and custom MCU; define DO reset-on-stop behavior on the control box if needed (`SetOutputResetCtlBoxDO` per Fairino manual).

```

All motion scripts are stored **locally on the edge PC** — the same machine that runs IceBot — under the **`workflow/`** directory (path configurable, default: `./workflow` relative to app).

- Each **step** = one `.lua` file (atomic robot action).
- Each step file defines a **start pose** (first `MoveJ`) and **end pose** (last meaningful position in that step).
- A full **order workflow** = multiple `.lua` files composed into a **queue**, executed as **one continuous motion path** when chained.
- Files are resolved **up front** when an order arrives — not fetched one-by-one after each script finishes.

### Script chaining rule (nối file Lua)

**Authoring convention:** each production step `.lua` file is written as a simple **2-point path** (start pose → end pose) plus whatever waits belong to that step (`WaitMs`, ...). It does **not** loop back to its own start pose at the end. IceBot does not parse or care about point names/comments inside the file — it just uploads and runs the file **top to bottom**, in full, via `FairinoLuaExecutor.RunScript`.

Because files are authored this way, chaining needs **no special merge step** — running each queued file's full content back-to-back (`ProgramRun` per file, in order) already produces one continuous path, since each file's start pose is wherever the previous file's motion ended:

```
File 1 (cup_s.lua):        A → B
File 2 (ice_chocolate_s.lua): B → C
File 3 (deliver_tray.lua):    C → D

Queued in order → arm runs: A → B → C → D  (continuous, no jump back)
```

The robot returns to its **home teaching point (`robot_home`)** at exactly two points, both handled automatically by `WorkflowRunner.RunQueue`: once at the **start** of a run (right after connecting — stands in for "just powered on / reset") and once at the **end** (after the whole queue finishes — "this item is done"). It does **not** return home between steps within one item. `robot_home` is **a named teaching point saved on the robot controller via the Fairino app — not a `.lua` file**; `FairinoLuaExecutor.MoveToTeachingPoint("robot_home")` reads it live from the controller (`GetRobotTeachingPoint`) and issues a blocking `MoveJ`. The point name is the `HomeTeachingPoint` constant in `WorkflowRunner`. IceBot moves home around the queue itself — the order→queue mapper does not need to add anything.

> ⚠️ The current `workflow/lay_coc.lua` in this repo is a **demo/test script** (FaiRobot Studio sample) — it round-trips A→B→A instead of following the 2-point convention above. Production step files must **not** replicate that pattern.

---

### Order → queue example

Customer order: *Chocolate ice cream, size S, topping rainbow sprinkles (kẹo cốm)*


| Step | Step name | Action |
|------|-----------|--------|
| 1 | `cup_s` | Arm runs `cup_s.lua` into position, **then** IceBot sends serial Dispense command over RS485 to the cup-dropping machine — cup drops into the gripper |
| 2 | `ice_chocolate_s.lua` | Dispense chocolate ice cream (S) — arm pose, **then** IceBot sends Motor Run UP over RS485 to the STM32 dispense board, hold ~5s |
| 3 | `topping_keo_com.lua` | Add rainbow sprinkles — arm pose, **then** IceBot triggers the topping machine over RS485 (not yet implemented — see Implementation status) |
| 4 | `deliver_tray.lua` | Place on tray for customer |

**Ordering now comes from BE, not IceBot.** BE already knows which flavor/topping/qty maps to
which `.lua` files and in what physical order they must run, so the `/api/orders` payload
(`OrderRequest`) carries `steps` pre-ordered: `["cup_s.lua", "ice_chocolate_s.lua",
"topping_keo_com.lua", "deliver_tray.lua"]`. IceBot only checks each file exists locally in
`workflow/`, then passes `steps` straight to `WorkflowRunner.RunQueue` — no order→step mapper,
no re-sorting of any kind (there used to be a `Position`-based `WorkflowQueueBuilder` for this;
it was removed once BE took over ordering). `WorkflowRunner` runs each `.lua` file on the arm in
that order (continuous motion, see chaining rule above); after `cup_s.lua` finishes, it
additionally calls `Trigger()` on the module registered for that step (`CupDroppingMachineModule`,
resolved via `MachineRegistry.TryGetModule`).

### Execution model (production)

Cloud server **cannot** reach the store LAN directly. Orders are **pushed to the robot controller** via public ingress:

```
Payment OK on cloud
    → POST order to robot controller
         via NetBird
         body: OrderRequest { orderId, steps: [ "cup_s.lua", "ice_chocolate_s.lua", ... ] }
         (BE already resolved which files + what order — no mapping logic on the edge)
    → IceBot validates every named file exists in local workflow/ (400 if not) → OrderQueue.Enqueue
    → single background worker thread calls WorkflowRunner.RunQueue(steps, ...) — serialized,
      so two orders never drive the arm at the same time
    → WorkflowRunner runs the queue in order, per step:
         1. LuaUpload → ProgramLoad → ProgramRun the step's .lua file on Fairino arm (192.168.58.2)
         2. Resolve the step's machine in MachineRegistry.Modules; if it implements
            IMachineTrigger (e.g. cup_s), resolve its COM port and call Trigger(comPort)
            right after — arm is already in position
    → Optional: POST status back to cloud (completed / failed) — not implemented yet
```

**Current:** Console menu + CLI; real operator login; mTLS Full Edge deployment pull and verified
Lua bundle installation; local API `serve` mode; RS485 peripheral triggers. Order execution still
uses the legacy inbound filename contract and status POST-back remains TODO.

## Store login (operator account)

Operator login is implemented against the real BE contract:

- `POST {BE_API_URL}/api/v1/authentication/login` with `emailOrUsername` and `password`.
- IceBot stores `BE_ACCESS_TOKEN` and the rotated `BE_REFRESH_TOKEN`; it does not retain the
  plaintext password after successful login.
- Startup attempts `POST /api/v1/authentication/refresh`; failure clears both tokens and returns
  to the blocking login prompt.
- Operator JWTs are for human-authorized operations only. They are deliberately not used for
  execution command pull, artifact download, heartbeat, ACK, or execution reports.

`BE_API_URL` is still a deployment placeholder until the BE private NetBird address is known.
Set it to the BE's private **HTTPS** base URL, without `/api`, through menu configuration,
`BE_API_URL` in `icebot.site.env`, or `ICEBOT_BE_API_URL`.

---

## Lua deployment synchronization (Full Edge)

The old `BeApi.GetLua(models)` mock is no longer the menu/CLI provisioning path. Backend does not
expose Lua bytes through a direct public REST endpoint. Full Edge uses the durable deployment flow:

```
Management creates a Full Edge deployment
    → IceBot POST /api/v1/iot/execution-endpoints/{endpointId}/commands/pull (mTLS)
    → BE returns DeployConfiguration with a short-lived FullEdgeBundle.DownloadUrl
    → IceBot downloads the ZIP directly from object storage
    → verify bundle byte length + SHA-256
    → safely inspect artifacts/{RobotArtifactId}.lua entries
    → verify every artifact byte length + SHA-256
    → install verified files and release-content-manifest.json into workflow/
    → durably save active deployment/release state
    → ACK Accepted, then report Installed and Active
```

Entry points: menu `Cau hinh > 4` or `IceBot.exe provision`.

### Required site configuration

| Setting | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `BE_API_URL` / `ICEBOT_BE_API_URL` | **TODO when discovered:** private HTTPS BE URL reachable through NetBird |
| `EXECUTION_ENDPOINT_ID` / `ICEBOT_EXECUTION_ENDPOINT_ID` | Active Full Edge execution endpoint provisioned by BE management |
| `EXECUTION_CLIENT_CERT_PATH` / `ICEBOT_EXECUTION_CLIENT_CERT_PATH` | Local PFX whose SHA-256 certificate fingerprint is pinned to the endpoint |
| `ICEBOT_EXECUTION_CLIENT_CERT_PASSWORD` | PFX password; environment-only, never written to `icebot.site.env` |

The BE must listen on its NetBird-reachable HTTPS address. Object storage configuration
`RobotArtifacts:ObjectStorage:DownloadEndpoint` must also produce a URL reachable from Edge;
a Docker-only hostname such as `minio:9000` is invalid outside the BE host.

### Installation guarantees and current boundary

- Maximum accepted bundle size is 100 MiB, matching BE.
- Nothing is written to the active workflow until the complete bundle and every Lua entry pass
  descriptor validation.
- Bundle entries are immutable GUID names (`artifacts/{RobotArtifactId}.lua`) per BE contract;
  local filenames are therefore `{RobotArtifactId}.lua`.
- `workflow/` remains gitignored and site-local.
- The legacy inbound `/api/orders` filename-based execution contract predates the BE's current
  artifact-ID/release-manifest contract. Lua deployment sync is implemented, but order execution
  still needs a separate migration to resolve BE artifact IDs from the active release manifest.

## User Interface

Simple command-line interface — robot arm control utility, not an end-user product.

### Main menu (`IceBot.exe`)

A **login gate runs before the menu** (see "Store login" above) — blocking, loops until
`BeApi.Login` succeeds. Only after that does the menu below appear.

Main menu is 4 lines; items `1` and `2` open their own submenu, which **renumbers from 1** (not
a literal `1.1` keystroke — this doc uses "1.1" style dotted notation purely to describe nested
location in prose, e.g. "1.2" = main item 1 ("Cau hinh") → submenu item 2 ("Cau hinh he thong")).

| # | Action |
|---|--------|
| 1 | **Cau hinh** — opens submenu |
| 2 | **Test may** — opens submenu |
| 3 | Chay he thong — `serve` mode (nhan don tu BE) |
| 0 | Thoat |

Submenu "Cau hinh" (enter via main `1`; header prints `CAU HINH`) — split into two separate
wizard entry points (`ConfigSetupWizard.RunNetBird()` / `RunSystemSettings()`) precisely so
NetBird's own config doesn't get bundled with unrelated settings:

| # | Action |
|---|--------|
| 1 | Cau hinh NetBird — ONLY `NetBirdSetupKey` + `PublicUrl` (`ConfigSetupWizard.RunNetBird`) |
| 2 | Cau hinh he thong — API key, robot IP, tai khoan cua hang, cong COM may ngoai vi (`ConfigSetupWizard.RunSystemSettings`) |
| 3 | Xem cau hinh hien tai |
| 4 | Đồng bộ Full Edge deployment từ BE qua mTLS; tải và xác minh Lua bundle |
| 0 | Quay lai (main menu) |

Submenu "Test may" (enter via main `2`; header prints `TEST MAY`) — deliberately just 2 items,
each doing connection-only checks (no manual Query/Trigger picker anymore — that flow was
removed):

| # | Action |
|---|--------|
| 1 | **Test tay Robot** — two independent steps: (a) `FairinoLuaExecutor.Connect`, plain connect/disconnect report; (b) load + run a sample `.lua` from `test-workflow/` (see "Provisioned steps & robot test sample"), skipped gracefully if missing or if (a) failed |
| 2 | **Test ket noi may ngoai vi (Serial)** — for each step name in `SiteSettings.ProvisionedSteps`, resolve via `MachineRegistry.TryGetModule`, call `TestConnection` if it's an `IMachineTrigger`; prints `{step} : connect` or `{step} : disconnect (reason)`. Steps with no RS485 driver are silently skipped |
| 0 | Quay lai (main menu) |

Implementation: `ConsoleMenu.Run()` (main), `ConsoleMenu.RunConfigMenu()`, `ConsoleMenu.RunTestMenu()`, `ConsoleMenu.RunTestMode()` (item 1), `ConsoleMenu.RunPeripheralConnectionTestMode()` (item 2).

## Network / Connection

### LAN — IceBot ↔ Fairino arm

| Item | Value |
|------|--------|
| Fairino arm control box IP | **`192.168.58.2`** |
| Override | Optional CLI flag if needed |

Robot controller (edge PC) and Fairino arm must be on the same LAN (`192.168.58.x`).

### Cloud ↔ Robot controller (production) — NetBird

**Chosen stack (2026-07-31): NetBird** (the real https://netbird.io product — WireGuard-based
mesh network, not a project-specific API) — replaces the earlier DuckDNS + Cloudflare Tunnel
stack (dynamic DNS *and* the tunnel itself, both in one). IceBot's side of this is a setup key
(`NetBirdSetupKey` / `NETBIRD_SETUP_KEY`, entered at menu Cau hinh > 1 as "NetBird setup key")
that NetBird uses to identify this store and open the path in. Unlike the rest of the BE-facing
surface (mock-only for now), **NetBird is real and IceBot actively drives its CLI end to end**,
including installing it:

`Config/NetBirdSetup.cs`:
- `ResolveExecutable()` — tries bare `"netbird"` (works if it resolves via this process's
  PATH), else checks the known install path `%ProgramFiles%\Netbird\netbird.exe` directly on
  disk. The disk check matters: a Windows process that was already running when NetBird's
  installer updated the system PATH never sees that update (inherited env is a snapshot from
  process start) — checking the file's existence on disk sidesteps that entirely.
- If neither resolves → **auto-installs NetBird** via `winget install --id Netbird.Netbird
  --silent --accept-package-agreements --accept-source-agreements` (3 min timeout), then
  resolves again. This is the concrete implementation of "may Edge tu dong cai NetBird cho
  nguoi dung" — no manual install step, no separate terminal.
- Then runs `netbird up --setup-key <key>` (1 min timeout) and surfaces NetBird's own
  stdout/stderr as the result message (`[OK]`/`[WARN]`/`[ERROR]`, never throws past the caller).
- Both winget install and the driver setup NetBird performs typically need **Administrator**
  rights; a non-interactive process can't answer a UAC prompt, so instead of hanging forever
  each child process has a timeout and is killed, reporting "may dang cho quyen admin (UAC)" —
  the fix is running `IceBot.exe` elevated.

**Two call sites, both non-blocking** (report and continue, matching the "warn, don't gate"
pattern used for other missing config — login is the one exception that blocks):
1. `ConfigSetupWizard.RunNetBird()` — right after prompting for the setup key, only if it's new/changed
   from what was already saved.
2. `ConsoleMenu.EnsureNetBirdConnected()` — called at the top of **both** `ConsoleMenu.Run()`
   (interactive menu) and `ConsoleMenu.RunServeMode()` (`serve`), immediately after
   `StoreAuth.RequireLogin()`, whenever a setup key is already saved. This is what makes a
   **fresh Edge PC image** work correctly: the key can be provisioned ahead of time (e.g. baked
   into the image or entered once), and the very first `IceBot.exe` launch on that machine
   installs NetBird and connects — no wizard re-entry required.

| Component | Role |
|-----------|------|
| **NetBird** | Opens the path from cloud BE to this Edge PC; identifies the store via `NetBirdSetupKey` |
| **IceBot `serve` mode** | `IceBot.exe serve` — local HTTP API NetBird routes into |

```
Cloud BE
    → POST https://ice-shop.example.com/api/orders   (via NetBird)
    → NetBird → localhost:5080
    → IceBot LocalApiServer
    → workflow/ → Fairino arm @ 192.168.58.2
```

**Deploy files:** `deploy/icebot/start-serve.ps1`. `deploy/duckdns/` and `deploy/cloudflare/`
are still in the repo but **stale** — leftover from the old ingress stack, no NetBird
equivalent written yet (NetBird's actual deploy/setup mechanism isn't known to this codebase).

**Env vars (robot controller):**

| Variable | Purpose |
|----------|---------|
| `ICEBOT_NETBIRD_SETUP_KEY` | NetBird setup key for this store |
| `ICEBOT_PUBLIC_URL` | Public URL BE calls into (assigned via NetBird) |
| `ICEBOT_BE_API_URL` | **Private HTTPS BE base URL through NetBird — value still pending discovery** |
| `ICEBOT_EXECUTION_ENDPOINT_ID` | Active Full Edge execution endpoint GUID provisioned in BE |
| `ICEBOT_EXECUTION_CLIENT_CERT_PATH` | Local mTLS client certificate PFX path |
| `ICEBOT_EXECUTION_CLIENT_CERT_PASSWORD` | PFX password; environment-only, never persisted |
| `ICEBOT_API_KEY` | Shared secret; `X-Api-Key` header |
| `ICEBOT_ROBOT_IP` | Fairino arm IP (default `192.168.58.2`) |

Config file: `config/icebot.site.env` (gitignored, next to `IceBot.exe`).

## Input: LUA Script Format

Scripts are standard Lua files compatible with the Fairino controller runtime.

### Script structure (per file)

Each workflow `.lua` file is authored as a standalone step with:

- **Start point** — first `MoveJ` in the file (used only when this file runs alone, or as file 1 in a chain).
- **Body** — intermediate moves, `WaitMs`, etc. Peripheral machines are **not** triggered from inside the `.lua` file — IceBot (C#) sends that command over RS485 after the file finishes (see Peripheral machine control).
- **End point** — position where the step finishes; becomes the implicit start for the next chained file.

When chaining, only the **first `MoveJ`** of files 2..N is stripped. All other commands (`MoveJ`, `WaitMs`, …) are kept in order.

---
Scripts typically include a header block with project name, robot model, date, and SDK compatibility note.

### Utility: `toDouble()`

Fairino LUA runtime may parse bare integers as integer type. Scripts wrap numeric literals through `toDouble()` so values are always treated as double-precision floats:

```lua
local function toDouble(v)
    return tonumber(tostring(v)) + 0.0
end
```

### Supported commands (from sample)

| Command | Purpose | Example |
|---------|---------|---------|
| `MoveJ` | Joint-space move to 6 joint angles (degrees) | `MoveJ({j1..j6}, 0, 0, speed, acc, -1.0, -1.0)` |
| `WaitMs` | Pause execution (milliseconds) | `WaitMs(5000)` |

Peripheral machine control (`SetDO`/DO trigger) is **not** part of the current design — every
peripheral triggers over RS485 from IceBot (C#) after the `.lua` file finishes, not from a
command inside the file (see Peripheral machine control above).

### `MoveJ` parameters (sample pattern)

```
MoveJ(
  {j1, j2, j3, j4, j5, j6},  -- 6 joint angles (degrees)
  0, 0,                        -- flags / blend (per SDK)
  speed, acc,                  -- e.g. 30.0, 30.0
  -1.0, -1.0                   -- tool / user frame (default)
)
```

### Sample workflow (`lay_coc.lua`)

1. Move to position A (home-like pose)
2. Move to position B (work pose)
3. Wait 5 seconds (`WaitMs(5000)`)
4. Move to position B again
5. Move to position A (return)

### Design change (2026-07-31): ordering moved from IceBot to BE

Original design had IceBot mapping order contents (flavor/topping/qty) to step names itself,
then sorting them via a `Position` field on `IMachineModule` + a `WorkflowQueueBuilder` that
sorted steps into physical line order. **This was replaced**: BE now resolves both which
`.lua` files an order needs *and* the exact run order, and sends that list directly in `steps`.
IceBot's responsibility shrank to: validate the named files exist locally, then run them in the
given order — no mapping logic, no re-sorting. `Position`, `WorkflowQueueBuilder.cs`, and its
tests were deleted (not just left unused) — there is no machine-ordering feature in IceBot
anymore; `IMachineModule` only carries identity (`MachineType`, `DisplayName`, `StepNames`).

**Lưu ý:**
- `WorkflowRunner.RunQueue` is blocking — `OrderQueue` runs it on a single dedicated background
  thread (not the HTTP thread), which also guarantees two orders never drive the arm at once.
- Home return at start/end is automatic inside `RunQueue` — BE's `steps` list does not need a
  home step.
- `WorkflowRunner.RunQueue` is also called from menu 2.1 / `test` command in `Cli/ConsoleMenu.cs`
  with the hardcoded `AppConfig.TestScriptQueue` — unaffected by this change.

### Site setup

1. **Provision endpoint** in BE management and place its PFX on Edge.
2. **Set private connectivity** — add the private NetBird HTTPS BE URL and ensure the presigned object-storage host is Edge-reachable.
3. **Synchronize Lua** — menu configuration item 4 or `IceBot.exe provision` pulls a pending deployment and installs only fully verified artifacts.

### Runtime (orders)

1. **Receive order** from cloud (HTTP on robot controller, via NetBird) — body is `OrderRequest` (`orderId` + BE-ordered `steps`, no home step needed since `WorkflowRunner` adds `robot_home` automatically at start and end).
2. **Validate** every named file exists in local `workflow/` (400 `missing_lua_file` if not).
3. **Enqueue** — `OrderQueue.Enqueue` hands the order to a single background worker thread (serializes runs; never two orders driving the arm at once) and the HTTP handler returns 202 immediately.
4. **Execute** — `WorkflowRunner.RunQueue` moves to the `robot_home` teaching point first, then runs each queued step's `.lua` on the Fairino arm in the order BE sent (chaining is automatic since files are simple 2-point paths — see script chaining rule; if the step's machine in `MachineRegistry` implements `IMachineTrigger`, call its `Trigger()` right after), then moves back to `robot_home` at the end.
5. **Log / report** — console + optional status POST back to cloud *(❌ TODO — not implemented yet)*.

### Robot execution

Fairino C# SDK on robot controller: connect to arm @ `192.168.58.2` → for each queued step, `LuaUpload` → `ProgramRun` that step's `.lua` in full → poll until complete → (optionally) fire that step's peripheral trigger.

## Out of Scope (until specified)

- Complex GUI (WPF, WinForms, web frontend).
- Generating LUA scripts (handled by FaiRobot Studio or external tools).
- Real-time teleoperation outside of scripted moves.
- Multi-robot orchestration.
